# Code doc comments

Doc comments are reference for someone calling the code, so they describe the contract and never the machinery behind it.

## Learn the conventions first

Syntax, tags, placement and link format differ per language, so take them from these sources, in order.

1. The project's instruction files for that language (*e.g.* a `go.instructions.md`, a style guide).
2. The existing doc comments of the same package or module, which show what the project already settled on.
3. The language's official documentation guide.

When those disagree, follow the earlier source in that list and mention the difference in the report.

## Content

- The first sentence names the symbol and says what it returns, or what it does when called for its effect.
- One sentence is enough when the name and signature hide nothing else.
- Following paragraphs cover what a caller can't guess, such as where the symbol departs from what its name suggests.
- Cover the defaults, special inputs, errors and concurrency guarantees that apply to the symbol.
- Give what the caller must do as an imperative ("Don't close it yourself"), and say what is not an error or not guaranteed.
- Name the simpler alternative when the symbol is rarely the right choice.
- Cover the contrast with a sibling symbol (*e.g.* "Unlike Load, a missing file returns the default configuration instead of an error").
- Reference other symbols with the language's own link syntax instead of repeating what they do.
- Put a package or module overview where the language expects it, with a short example that runs as written.
- Ask before adding a file for it.
- Mark a deprecated symbol with the language's deprecation form, saying what to use instead.

## What stays out

- How the code works inside (algorithm, data structures, call order), which goes in a comment inside the code, and only as a non-obvious fact.
- Why the design was chosen, which belongs in the change description.
- A step-by-step workflow, which belongs in a README or a docs page.

Language-mandated doc comments may run several sentences, unlike inline comments.
Each sentence still has to tell the caller something the signature doesn't.

## Inline comments

- These are defaults, and the project's own comment rules win where they differ.
- Write none by default, and add one only for a non-obvious fact (a hidden constraint, a subtle invariant, a bug workaround).
- Cap it at one sentence.
- Wrap a comment line at the formatter's limit when the language has one.
- Where the formatter sets none (gofmt for comments), keep each line readable at a glance.
- Split a line much longer than its neighbors at a transition word.
- End a comment on its own line with a period, unless it is a structural marker (*e.g.* `// Arrange`), and never end a trailing comment with one.
- Never mention the replaced implementation or the history.
- State a fact once, at its definition, never again in a sibling or a nearby comment.

## Review

- When a change touches a symbol, re-read the doc comments of that symbol and of its callers' public API.
- Fix any sentence the change made false.
